title: Ambassador of Palestine Asks Mexico to Review Companies Linked to Israeli Settlements
author: Georgina Saldierna and Néstor Jiménez
content:
_This article by[Georgina Saldierna and Néstor
Jiménez](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Georgina%20Saldierna%20y%20N%C3%A9stor%20Jim%C3%A9nez)
originally appeared in the [October 5, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/05/politica/embajadora-de-
palestina-pide-a-mexico-revisar-empresas-vinculadas-a-asentamientos-
israelies), Mexico's premier left wing daily newspaper._

**Mexico City**. The ambassador of Palestine to Mexico, Nadya Rasheed, asked
Mexico to **review the value chains of those national corporations linked to
Israel 's settlements** in Palestinian territory, in order to guarantee that
trade and investment do not benefit those areas and that Mexican companies do
not contribute to or profit from activities that, she said, sustain the
occupation.

In a meeting with the president of the Senate, Higinio Martínez, she
highlighted Mexico's support for Palestine and its consistent defense of
international law.

> But it is not international law that we lack. What has been lacking are
> consequences when that law is systematically violated.
>
> Nadya Rasheed, Ambassador of Palestine to Mexico

She recalled that the International Court of Justice has determined that
Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory is illegal
and must come to an end as soon as possible. It has also made clear that
states have the obligation not to recognize or contribute to maintaining this
illegal situation and must distinguish, in their relations, between Israel and
the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967.

The ambassador noted that governments have begun to be seen translating these
obligations into concrete measures. For example, last month, **12 countries,
among them Canada, France and the United Kingdom, announced restrictions on
trade** with the illegal Israeli settlements.

Nadya Rasheed considered it possible to guarantee that there is no commercial
exchange with those areas, to sanction those who carry out settler violence
and those who facilitate it, and to ensure that companies do not profit from
the occupation and from the illegal expansion of the settlements.

This is one of the areas in which she said she hopes to work closely with the
Senate to analyze what additional measures Mexico can adopt, “including the
review of the value chains of those national corporations whose links to the
settlement economy have been pointed out by the UN, in order to guarantee that
trade and investment do not benefit the illegal settlements and that Mexican
companies do not contribute to or profit from activities that sustain the
occupation.”

It is not about, she said, punishing or isolating a country. It is about
guaranteeing that international law has meaning.

She added that, when violations of international law have no consequences and
continue, the credibility of the entire international system is weakened.

She expressed confidence in working together with the senators to translate
“our shared principles into concrete actions, because we cannot wait for there
to be less Palestine left to protect.”

Higinio Martínez said that the Senate will do its part and that he will convey
the diplomat's message to his colleagues. He committed to continue working so
that there is peace in Gaza, in the Middle East and throughout the world.

The UN has identified 214 companies linked to Israel's settlements in
Palestinian territory, among them **the Mexican conglomerate Orbia**.
